=== PUCT 58482 - EDF comments on LLDM Service 04.08.26.pdf ===
                                         PROJECT NO. 58482


    LARGE LOAD DEMAND MANAGEMENT §                             PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    SERVICE UNDER PURA § 39.170(b) §                                       OF
                                   §                                     TEXAS


        ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND’S COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO
      COMMISSION STAFF QUESTIONS RELATING TO LARGE LOAD DEMAND
              MANAGEMENT SERVICE UNDER PURA § 39.170(b)


Environmental Defense Fund (“EDF”) files the following comments in response to Commission
Staff’s questions for comment issued March 23, 2026 (“Staff Questions”), related to options being
considered to implement a large load demand management service pursuant to PURA § 39.170(b).
Commission Staff requested comments be filed by April 8, 2026, so these comments are timely
filed. Consistent with instructions in the Staff Questions, an Executive Summary is appended to
these comments.

     I. INTRODUCTION

As a general matter, EDF supports electric system load management, which can help drive down
infrastructure costs, improve system reliability and resiliency, and reduce health-harming
emissions from electricity generation. The ERCOT region faces a particularly acute need for more
load management across all end-use sectors, including but not necessarily limited to large loads,
in light of its rapid projected load growth.1

For example, Aurora Energy Research’s study on resource adequacy needs in ERCOT found that
if 60% of data center loads were flexible under a high load growth scenario, with 10% being price
responsive and 50% providing emergency and ancillary services during EEA2 conditions, they
would help fully avoid load shed events under both extreme winter and summer weather events
and save the system $3.7 billion.2 Similarly, modeling by MIT’s Center for Energy and
Environmental Policy Research suggests that large loads equipped with temporal flexibility
materially improve ERCOT reliability by shifting demand away from peak and scarcity hours,
reducing ramping requirements and lowering system costs by up to 5%. The study also found that
unmanaged large loads pose reliability risks, but that those risks are effectively mitigated through
enforceable demand response rather than interconnection delays.3 With proper market mechanisms
in place, allowing large loads like data centers to function as reliability resources, rather than
passive demand, offers a new pool of resources that can provide enough demand response to
1
  Data center load is anticipated to grow over 24GW by 2031 under ERCOT’s Longterm Load Forecast. See
https://www.ercot.com/gridinfo/load/forecast (retrieved April 7, 2026).
2
  Aurora Energy Research, Assessment of Resource Adequacy Needs in ERCOT and Impact of Market Design
Changes at 11 (November 10, 2025), https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/12/10/Aurora-Assessment-of-
Resource-Adequacy-Needs-in-ERCOT-Region-and-Impact-of-Market-Design-Changes-2025.11.10-.pdf.
3
  Knittel et al., Flexible Data Centers and the Grid: Lower Costs, Higher Emissions? MIT CEEPR Working Paper
2025-14 (July 2025), https://ceepr.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/MIT-CEEPR-WP-2025-14.pdf.
 mitigate load-shedding during times of grid stress. The Commission should seek in this proceeding
to optimize cost-effective participation in a new large load demand management service, consistent
with the near-term needs of the ERCOT system, to create net cost and reliability benefits.

As a threshold matter, the Commission should not (and need not) apply an overly-prescriptive
interpretation of PURA § 39.170(b) that would frustrate this objective. As the Staff Questions
observe, PURA § 39.170(b)(3) provides that the new service must “prohibit participation by any
large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity, as determined by
the independent organization certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region, or that
otherwise participates in a different reliability or ancillary service.” This does not mean that load
that responds to any form of price signal – such as payments under a large load demand response
service – is necessarily ineligible to participate. Such a circular interpretation would necessarily
make it impossible to establish a market-based mechanism to incent large load curtailment, thereby
defeating the purpose and intent of PURA § 39.170.4 EDF encourages the Commission to apply
an interpretation of PURA § 39.170(b)(3) that strikes a reasonable balance between supporting
system reliability and minimizing duplicative payments to participating customers, as discussed
further herein.


    II. QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

In the interest of brevity, EDF’s comments herein are limited to certain issues. EDF’s silence on
any question at this time does not indicate EDF’s position thereon, and EDF reserves all rights to
comment on any issue in the future.

1. Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?

A seasonal service is the better option because it is comparatively more likely to attract meaningful
customer participation. Much of the value of this large load demand management service will
derive from ERCOT’s ability to require curtailed loads to remain offline until emergency
conditions ease. Thus, whether the service is procured seasonally or as-needed, curtailment for
each event will likely include some degree of duration unpredictability. This can pose a challenge
to loads eligible to offer the service, which (by definition) are those that are mostly non-responsive
to price – that is, they place a high value on not being curtailed.

EDF expects that such customers would seldom opt to participate in an as-needed service. Under
an as-needed service structure, ERCOT would procure the service – i.e., solicit customers’
promises to curtail – shortly before an emergency event. A customer deciding whether to
participate will essentially be choosing between two options: (1) decline to offer such a promise
and remain online, with the understanding that they may ultimately face exposure to the

4
 Indeed, such an interpretation would render PURA’s language establishing large load demand response service
“mere surplusage,” in contravention of Texas canons of statutory construction. See Nguyen v. Watts, 605 S.W.3d
761, 777 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] May 28, 2020) (“We give effect to all the statute’s words and, if possible,
do not treat any statutory language as mere surplusage. We presume there is a purpose for every word and clause
used . . . .”).

                                                         2
 $5000/MWh wholesale electricity price cap and a high transmission charge during some portion
of the event; or (2) agree to curtail for an unspecified period of time in exchange for payment. EDF
would expect many or most customers faced with this decision would choose option #1, because
not curtailing would provide comparatively more certainty, and would enable them to maintain
operations whose outputs may be more valuable than even very high energy cost inputs. Moreover,
in such a scenario, those few customers willing to accept curtailment would probably be able to
demand an extremely high price for it.

Conversely, a seasonal approach would probably appeal to more eligible customers. When
assessing participation in a seasonal service, a customer’s evaluation would include the likelihood
of curtailment events (unlike under an as-needed scenario, where curtailment is effectively
guaranteed once an event is triggered). The introduction of this additional factor would allow
prospective participants to hedge – that is, to weigh the value of uninterrupted operations against
the value of their net curtailment risk. EDF expects that this would enable more customers to
submit bids, and for average bids to be lower, as compared to an as-needed structure.

Additionally, a seasonal approach would offer more predictability to both ERCOT and
participating customers. It would enable ERCOT to establish the quantity of available demand
management service well in advance of an emergency condition, and to plan its operations
accordingly. It would also allow ERCOT to coordinate procurement of this service with its
procurements of Emergency Response Service, as the Staff Questions contemplate, which may
yield reliability and cost benefits. On the customer side, a seasonal approach would relieve eligible
customers from needing to decide, in a short (and probably hectic) pre-curtailment-event window,
whether to submit a bid and for how much. A seasonal structure would allow participating
customers to use that pre-curtailment window to focus on their internal process steps needed to
curtail their loads.

The main drawback to a seasonal structure is that it relies on longer-term forecasts to set the
quantity to procure, which will tend to be less precise than as-needed quantities established
immediately prior to an emergency event. Setting the quantity too high (i.e., overprocuring the
new service) may unnecessarily inflate total costs, even if the average unit cost is lower. Setting
the quantity too low (underprocurement) will necessitate more reliance on other mechanisms
during emergency conditions. But ERCOT’s experience conducting resource adequacy
assessments (as discussed in response to Question #4 below) mitigates this drawback, and on
balance, EDF believes that it constitutes a worthwhile trade-off in exchange for the other benefits
of a seasonal structure.


2. PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA §
39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods when the
service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.

       a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances other
       than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?



                                                 3
 Yes, PURA authorizes ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances other than extreme
weather events. The statute’s use of different terms “anticipated emergency condition” at PURA §
39.170(b) and “extreme weather events” PURA § 39.170(b)(1) demonstrates that those two terms
are not synonymous. Specifically, “extreme weather events” constitute one non-exclusive category
of “anticipated emergency condition” that may trigger deployment of the new service.

EDF recommends a standard for “anticipated emergency condition” based on electric system
conditions, rather than focusing on only certain factors that affect electric system conditions.
Specifically, the Commission should adopt a definition that allows ERCOT to deploy the new
service before operating reserves are expected to drop below 2,500 MW for at least 30 minutes
(i.e., Energy Emergency Alert (“EEA”) Level 1 conditions), irrespective of the drivers of the
system emergency. At this time, EDF does not recommend a specific threshold that should trigger
service deployment, as such threshold(s) will likely depend in part on other aspects of the design
of the service.

       b. Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how should it be
       defined?

The Commission need not define “extreme weather event” because ERCOT’s deployment of the
new service should be triggered by “anticipated emergency conditions,” not any single driver (such
as weather) of such anticipated emergency.


3. PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit participation
by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity, as
determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a different reliability or ancillary
service. PURA § 37.0561(e)-which allows ERCOT to direct a large load customer with onsite
backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its backup generation under certain
circumstances-states that a large load customer with onsite backup generation may
participate in a service authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).

       a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
       customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

EDF offers no comment at this time.

       b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should
       apply to participation in the new service?

EDF offers no comment at this time.

       c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four
       coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new
       service?




                                                4
 Under certain circumstances, a customer’s responsiveness to transmission scarcity pricing should
preclude their participation in the new service. EDF suggests using ERCOT’s High System-Wide
Offer Cap (HCAP) of $5000/MWh as a guiding factor in determining whether a customer should
be considered price-responsive and therefore ineligible to provide the new service. Where a
customer curtails its own load in response to transmission scarcity such that it realizes $5000/MWh
or less in avoided unitized costs (i.e., including avoided transmission charges converted to their
per-MWh equivalent), such behavior suggests that existing market mechanisms already suffice to
incent the customer to curtail. Conversely, where a customer’s behavior during periods of
transmission scarcity suggests that it values its electric service at more than $5000/MWh, the large
load demand management service may be needed to incent curtailment.

        d. Should the commission define "curtailment in response to wholesale price of
        electricity" and, if so, how should it be defined?

EDF offers no comment at this time.


4. How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

EDF anticipates that periodic competitive solicitations (e.g., auctions) will generally represent the
most efficient mechanism to establish budget and price of the new service, particularly under a
seasonal-procurement structure.

Such auction approach will amplify the importance of setting an appropriate target quantity for the
new service. EDF is not currently aware of an effective market mechanism for setting the target
quantity; the quantity will instead probably need to be administratively established. The
particularly method for setting the quantity warrants further in-depth consideration. As an initial
matter, parties could assess whether ERCOT’s Monthly Outlook for Resource Adequacy (MORA)
methodology,5 which identifies periods and probabilistic likelihoods of future EEA conditions on
a rolling basis, could be leveraged to also forecast the quantity of large load demand management
that would be needed to reduce EEA likelihood to an acceptable level.


5. What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of
PURA § 39.170(b)?

In implementing PURA § 39.170(b), the Commission should consider how the program structure
could support other forms of load management. The Commission and ERCOT are currently
considering demand management from several angles, including ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed
Energy Resource (ADER) Pilot Project6 and Residential Demand Response Program,7 the
capabilities of Emergency Response Service,8 and transmission cost allocation.9

5
  See generally https://www.ercot.com/gridinfo/resource.
6
  See https://www.ercot.com/mktrules/pilots/ader.
7
  ERCOT NPRR 1296.
8
  PUCT Docket No. 53385.
9
  PUCT Docket No. 58484.

                                                           5
 As discussed above, the need for and value of load management – of all forms of load, irrespective
of customer type – is likely to increase as loads and generation costs continue to grow. Moreover,
there remain significant untapped load management opportunities among non-large loads. FERC
reports that residential and commercial customers together accounted for 16,701.71 MW of
potential retail peak-demand savings in 2023—more than half of total reported retail demand-
response potential.10 National building-sector research likewise indicates that the technical
potential is much larger, with prior studies estimating at least 150–200 GW of summer peak
reduction by 2030 and more recent modeling finding up to 181 GW of daily net peak reduction in
2030 and 208 GW by 2050 from combined building efficiency and flexibility.11

EDF recognizes that the Commission’s immediate obligation in this proceeding, pursuant to PURA
§ 39.170, is to establish a load management service for large loads. But this does not foreclose the
Commission from considering opportunities to use this proceeding to bolster or accommodate
potential future expansions of load management. The Commission should seek to use lessons or
data gathered over the course of implementing the new service to inform its and ERCOT’s parallel
efforts.

6. PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each electric
cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving a
transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the load
to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative, transmission and distribution
utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer with the customer to the extent feasible to
shed load in a coordinated manner. This subsection applies only to a load interconnected
after December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical load industrial customer,
as defined by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical natural gas facility under Section
38.074. Should the Commission include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA
§39.170(a)?

EDF offers no comment at this time.




10
   Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n, 2025 Assessment of Demand Response and Advanced Metering at Table 3-2 (2025),
https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2025-
12/25_Annual%20Assessment%20of%20Demand%20Response_1212.pdf.
11
   Jared Langevin et al., U.S. Building Energy Efficiency and Flexibility as an Electric Grid Resource, 5 Joule 2102
(2021).

                                                         6
    III. CONCLUSION

EDF thanks the Commission for its attention to this important matter and for the opportunity to
comment. Consistent with the instructions in the Staff Questions, please see following page for a
standalone Executive Summary.

Date: April 8, 2026

                                                    Respectfully Submitted,




                                                    Michael Zimmerman
                                                    Interim Director & Senior Attorney, Clean
                                                    Affordable Power
                                                    Environmental Defense Fund
                                                    512-691-3444
                                                    mzimmerman@edf.org




                                               7
 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND COMMENTS

-   Submitting Entity: Environmental Defense Fund

-   Summary of Substantive Recommendations:
       o Seasonal procurements of large load demand management service (“Service”) are
         preferable to an “as-needed” approach.
       o PURA allows ERCOT to deploy the Service in “anticipated emergency
         conditions” other than extreme weather events.
       o The Commission should adopt a definition or interpretation of “anticipated
         emergency condition” that enables ERCOT to deploy the Service before EEA
         Level 1 conditions, irrespective of the driver of the emergency condition.
       o ERCOT should consider using the High System-Wide Offer Cap (HCAP) of
         $5000/MWh as a guiding factor in determining whether a customer should be
         considered price-responsive and therefore ineligible to provide the Service.
       o Preferably, ERCOT should determine Service price and budget through
         competitive solicitations. ERCOT can administratively establish Service quantity.
       o The Commission should seek to use lessons or data gathered over the course of
         implementing the Service to support expansion of load management opportunities
         to other customer classes.

4. How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

EDF anticipates that periodic competitive solicitations (e.g., auctions) will generally represent the
most efficient mechanism to establish budget and price of the new service, particularly under a
seasonal-procurement structure.

Such auction approach will amplify the importance of setting an appropriate target quantity for the
new service. EDF is not currently aware of an effective market mechanism for setting the target
quantity; the quantity will instead probably need to be administratively established. The
particularly method for setting the quantity warrants further in-depth consideration. As an initial
matter, parties could assess whether ERCOT' s Monthly Outlook for Resource Adequacy (MORA)
methodology,5 which identifies periods and probabilistic likelihoods of future EEA conditions on
a rolling basis, could be leveraged to also forecast the quantity of large load demand management
that would be needed to reduce EEA likelihood to an acceptable level.


5. What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of
PURA § 39.170(b)?

In implementing PURA § 39.170(b), the Commission should consider how the program structure
could support other forms of load management. The Commission and ERCOT are currently
considering demand management from several angles, including ERCOT' s Aggregate Distributed
Energy Resource (ADER) Pilot Project6 and Residential Demand Response Program,7 the
capabilities of Emergency Response Service,8 and transmission cost allocation.9

 As discussed above, the need for and value of load management - of@1 forms of load, irrespective
of customer type - is likely to increase as loads and generation costs continue to grow. Moreover,
there remain significant untapped load management opportunities among non-large loads. FERC
reports that residential and commercial customers together accounted for 16,701.71 MW of
potential retail peak-demand savings in 2023-more than half of total reported retail demand-
response potential.10 National building-sector research likewise indicates that the technical
potential is much larger, with prior studies estimating at least 150-200 GW of summer peak
reduction by 2030 and more recent modeling finding up to 181 GW of daily net peak reduction in
2030 and 208 GW by 2050 from combined building efficiency and flexibility.11

EDF recognizes that the Commission' s immediate obligation in this proceeding, pursuant to PURA
§ 39.170, is to establish a load management service for large loads. But this does not foreclose the
Commission from considering opportunities to use this proceeding to bolster or accommodate
potential future expansions of load management. The Commission should seek to use lessons or
data gathered over the course of implementing the new service to inform its and ERCOT' s parallel
efforts.

-   Summary of Substantive Recommendations:
       o Seasonal procurements of large load demand management service ("Service") are
         preferable to an "as-needed" approach.
       o PURA allows ERCOT to deploy the Service in "anticipated emergency
         conditions" other than extreme weather events.
       o The Commission should adopt a definition or interpretation of"anticipated
         emergency condition" that enables ERCOT to deploy the Service before EEA
         Level 1 conditions, irrespective of the driver of the emergency condition.
       o ERCOT should consider using the High System-Wide Offer Cap (HCAP) of

         considered price-responsive and therefore ineligible to provide the Service.
       o Preferably, ERCOT should determine Service price and budget through
         competitive solicitations. ERCOT can administratively establish Service quantity.
